evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with stable COPD in primary and specialist care: spirometric diagnosis, Saudi Thoracic Society (STS) classes I–III (GOLD A, B, E), inhaled therapy, exacerbation prevention, oxygen, rehabilitation and follow-up. Verified against the STS COPD guideline 2025 (with GOLD 2024 cross-reference); inhaler doses and contraindications from STS Table 5 and US FDA prescribing information. Exacerbations are covered in the Acute Exacerbation of COPD topic.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: NICE NG115 and GOLD 2024 cross-referenced, not re-reviewed in detail for this version
Tiotropium DPI dosing frequency from standard label practice (STS gives strength only)

pathophysiology.summary: COPD is a common, preventable and treatable disease with persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7) caused by airway and/or alveolar abnormalities, usually from smoking or other noxious exposures.
keyMechanisms: Chronic inhalation of tobacco smoke (including shisha/water-pipe and passive smoke) or biomass fuel → neutrophilic and macrophage inflammation, oxidative stress and protease–antiprotease imbalance (STS).
Small-airway narrowing and mucus hypersecretion (chronic bronchitis) plus alveolar wall destruction (emphysema) → airflow limitation and air trapping/hyperinflation.
V/Q mismatch → hypoxaemia; chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale; secondary polycythaemia (STS).
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in young patients with little smoking exposure (STS).
Exacerbations accelerate lung-function decline and raise mortality — prevention is a core goal.

symptoms: Exertional breathlessness, chronic cough, sputum production in a person aged 40 or over with smoking or exposure history.
Wheeze, chest tightness; recurrent winter 'chest infections'.
Fatigue, weight loss, ankle swelling in advanced disease.
physicalSigns: Hyperinflated chest, prolonged expiration, wheeze, reduced breath sounds.
Cyanosis, raised JVP and peripheral oedema (cor pulmonale); cachexia.
redFlags: Two or more exacerbations or any hospital admission in the past year (Class III/Group E)
Persistent hypercapnia 2 weeks after an exacerbation (consider home NIV)
Peripheral oedema or haematocrit 55% or more (cor pulmonale/polycythaemia)
Haemoptysis or weight loss — exclude lung cancer

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Variable symptoms, marked bronchodilator reversibility, atopy, raised FeNO/eosinophils.
Raised NT-proBNP, echo abnormality; restrictive or normal spirometry.
Daily purulent sputum; CT bronchial dilatation.
Crackles, restrictive pattern, CT changes; TB endemic exposure.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: At diagnosis; repeat if symptoms change
ruleIn.expectedFinding: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 confirms COPD in context. Severity: mild FEV1 80% or more; moderate 50–79%; severe 30–49%; very severe below 30% predicted.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Required for diagnosis — symptoms alone are not enough (STS).
ruleIn.normalValue: FEV1/FVC 0.7 or more; FEV1 80% predicted or more

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm, grade and classify
actions: Spirometry: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with symptoms and exposure; grade severity by FEV1 % predicted.

Classify (STS Table 4): Class I — CAT below 10 or mMRC 0–1 and 0–1 exacerbations without admission (GOLD A); Class II — CAT 10 or more or mMRC 2 or more, same exacerbation history (GOLD B); Class III — 2 or more exacerbations or any hospitalisation in the past year (GOLD E).
Record eosinophil count, oximetry, BMI and comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, anxiety/depression, lung cancer).

clinicalManagement.title: Non-drug treatment for all
actions: Smoking cessation (cigarettes, shisha, vaping) — the most effective intervention.
Pulmonary rehabilitation — strongly recommended (STS); also after any admission.
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccination; inhaler technique and written self-management plan.

clinicalManagement.title: Inhaled maintenance by class
actions: All: short-acting reliever (salbutamol and/or ipratropium) as needed.
Class I: a long-acting bronchodilator (LAMA preferred over LABA alone; LABA alone is not marketed in Saudi Arabia).
Class II and III: LAMA plus LABA, preferably in one inhaler (STS).
Class III with frequent exacerbations or eosinophils 300 cells/µL or more: triple therapy ICS/LABA/LAMA (STS). Low eosinophils: stay on LABA/LAMA.
Avoid ICS without bronchodilators; weigh ICS pneumonia risk.

clinicalManagement.title: Still exacerbating despite inhalers
actions: Roflumilast for chronic bronchitis with severe disease and exacerbations (STS).
Azithromycin 250 mg daily or 500 mg three times weekly after 1 or more exacerbations and a hospitalisation in the past year (STS) — check ECG (QTc) and hearing.
Mucolytics as add-on, never alone (STS). Dupilumab for eosinophils above 300 with chronic bronchitis (specialist).

clinicalManagement.title: Oxygen and ventilation
actions: LTOT if PaO2 below 55 mmHg (7.3 kPa) or SaO2 below 88% at rest, or PaO2 55–60 with cor pulmonale, oedema or haematocrit 55% or more, after 2 months of optimised therapy.
Target resting PaO2 60–65 mmHg or SaO2 88–94%; usually 1–2.5 L/min by nasal cannula for at least 18 h/day; review at 3 months and 1 year.
Do not use LTOT for moderate desaturation not meeting criteria (STS).
Home NIV if still hypercapnic 2 weeks after an exacerbation (STS).

learningObjectives: Diagnose COPD with spirometry, classify it (STS I–III) and manage stable disease to reduce symptoms and exacerbations.

keyPoints: Spirometry is essential: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 post-bronchodilator.
Triple therapy for frequent exacerbators or eosinophils 300 or more.
LTOT only for PaO2 below 55 mmHg (or 55–60 with complications).
pitfalls: ICS monotherapy or ICS in low-eosinophil patients.
Poor inhaler technique mistaken for treatment failure.
Oxygen for moderate desaturation not meeting criteria.
Missing alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in young patients.

patientEducation: Recognise worsening breathlessness, sputum colour or volume change.
lifestyleAndDiet: Stop smoking and shisha; avoid biomass smoke and dust.
mdtReferrals: Respiratory specialist: diagnostic doubt, Class III, LTOT/NIV, young age, AAT deficiency, lung volume reduction.
dischargeCriteria: Not applicable — chronic outpatient care. After an exacerbation: stable, inhaler technique checked, LTOT need assessed, follow-up within a few weeks, rehabilitation referral (STS).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review 4–8 weeks after starting or changing inhalers, then at least annually (more often if severe): symptoms (CAT/mMRC), exacerbations, inhaler technique, adherence, smoking status, oximetry, spirometry as needed.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with symptoms and exposure
2 or more exacerbations or 1 or more hospitalisations in the past year
Class III or eosinophils 300 cells/µL or more
PaO2 below 55 mmHg (or 55–60 with cor pulmonale/oedema/haematocrit 55% or more), stable 2 months

adjustments: Capsule for inhalation only — do not swallow
monitoring: Dry mouth, urinary retention, narrow-angle glaucoma symptoms
